title: Review a component that renders a huge list without virtualization
description: Problem: Review a component that renders a huge list without virtualization. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: **Review a component that renders a huge list without virtualization** is a classic frontend performance trap. A component that maps over thousands of items and renders them all at once creates a proportional number of DOM nodes. Each node consumes memory, participates in layout, and adds work to every subsequent render. The symptom is sluggish scrolling, delayed input, and eventually a frozen UI. The fix is almost always the same: render only what is visible.
Why huge lists break the UI

items: Every item in the array creates a DOM node, so 10,000 items means 10,000 nodes
React must diff the entire list on every state change, even for changes far from the viewport
Layout and paint costs grow linearly with DOM size, not with visible area
Event handlers attached to thousands of nodes increase memory pressure and GC churn
Scrolling performance degrades because the browser must composite a massive layer tree
Mobile browsers hit memory limits faster, causing tab termination

terms.definition: Rendering only the visible subset of a large list so the DOM size stays constant regardless of data length.
The number of items visible in the viewport plus a small overscan buffer.
Extra rows rendered above and below the visible window to reduce blank space during fast scrolling.
Interleaving DOM reads and writes, forcing the browser to recalculate layout repeatedly during a single frame.
React's algorithm for comparing the new virtual DOM tree with the previous one to determine which DOM nodes to update.

data.text: The telltale sign is a `.map()` that returns a large chunk of JSX without any slicing, filtering, or pagination. Another smell is an inline object or function inside the map, which creates a new reference on every render and defeats child memoization. In a code review, ask the author: 'What happens when this list grows to 50,000 items?' If they have not considered it, the component is not production-ready.

data.title: Unvirtualized list
data.content: This component renders every row at once. Scroll performance degrades as the dataset grows:

data.title: Popular approaches
items: react-window: lightweight, fixed or variable size lists with `FixedSizeList` and `VariableSizeList`
react-virtuoso: automatic size measurement, group support, and smooth scrolling out of the box
@tanstack/react-virtual: headless utility that gives you the visible range and lets you render it however you like
Custom windowing: calculate `startIndex` and `endIndex` from `scrollTop` and render a slice with absolute positioning
Pagination: send chunks from the server and render one page at a time
Infinite scroll: load more as the user scrolls, but still virtualize the rendered window

cards.title: Full render
cards.description: Render every item in the array as a DOM node.

cards.title: Virtualization
cards.description: Render only the visible window plus overscan.
pros: Smooth scrolling at any list length

cards.title: Pagination
cards.description: Load and render one page at a time.

cards.title: Infinite scroll
cards.description: Append items as the user scrolls toward the bottom.

data.title: Virtualization is not free
data.text: Virtualization adds complexity around scroll position restoration, dynamic row heights, and keyboard accessibility. If your list is under fifty items, the engineering cost usually outweighs the benefit. Choose virtualization when the dataset regularly exceeds five hundred rows.

A virtualized list wraps the visible items in a container whose height equals the full dataset height. An inner viewport is translated vertically based on scroll offset, and only the rows inside the visible window are rendered. The outer container preserves the native scrollbar, so the user experience is identical to a full list.

data.caption: Virtualized list render cycle
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Total items: 10,000] --> B[Calculate window height]
    B --> C[Calculate visible range from scrollTop]
    C --> D[Render only visible items + overscan]
    D --> E[Position inner container with translateY]
    E --> F[Outer container keeps full scroll height]
    F --> G[Browser paints a constant number of DOM nodes]
    G --> H[User scrolls smoothly regardless of data size]

data.title: FixedSizeList with overscan
data.content: Wrap the same rows in react-window. The DOM stays at roughly twenty nodes regardless of list length:

items: Ensure keyboard users can scroll the list with arrow keys and Page Up/Down
Provide a skip-to-content link so screen-reader users do not navigate through thousands of rows
Preserve scroll position when data updates or filters change
Handle dynamic row heights by measuring content or using a library that does it for you
Announce loading states for screen readers when new data is fetched

data.title: Virtualize a large table
data.description: Take an existing table component that renders 2,000 rows. Replace the full render with react-window or react-virtuoso. Measure scroll frames per second before and after with Chrome DevTools Performance panel.
steps: Identify the current full-list render and note the row height
Install react-window and wrap the rows in FixedSizeList
Adjust itemSize, height, and overscanCount until scrolling feels smooth
Profile the scroll interaction and confirm frame rate is above 55fps
Add keyboard navigation and test with a screen reader
data.expectedOutcome: The list should scroll smoothly with a constant DOM node count, and screen-reader users should be able to navigate without traversing every hidden row.

items.question: When should I reach for virtualization?
items.answer: When the dataset regularly exceeds five hundred items and the user scrolls through it. For smaller lists, the complexity is rarely worth it.

items.question: What about dynamic row heights?
items.answer: Use react-virtuoso or @tanstack/react-virtual, which measure content automatically. With react-window, you can use VariableSizeList but must provide accurate heights up front or accept visual jumps.

items.question: Does virtualization break search indexing or SEO?
items.answer: Not usually. Server-side rendered content is still in the HTML; virtualization only affects the client-side DOM count. If you client-render the entire list, you already have an SEO problem.

items.question: Should I virtualize a table or just paginate?
items.answer: Paginate when users need to compare rows across pages or export data. Virtualize when users scan sequentially and need fluid scrolling.

data.title: Summary
points: Full-list rendering becomes a performance liability above five hundred items
Virtualization keeps the DOM size constant by rendering only the visible window
Use a library like react-window, react-virtuoso, or @tanstack/react-virtual
Profile scroll performance before and after to confirm the improvement
Address keyboard navigation, screen readers, and scroll restoration
data.takeaway: A senior review catches unvirtualized lists not because they are always broken, but because they are a time bomb that grows worse with data.
